5864: Pelagic species presence at Manta Bowl, a submerged coastal seamount within the Ticao Burias Pass Protected Seascape (TBPPS), was investigated using remote underwater video surveys. Globally renowned as a reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi) cleaning station, this coastal seamount also hosts other endangered and protected species of megafauna including whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris), scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini), and pelagic thresher sharks (Alopias pelagicus). This study discusses the presence of pelagic thresher sharks at Manta Bowl. Pelagic thresher sharks are classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and are vulnerable to overexploitation due to their Kselected life-history traits. This study took place between August 2018 and August 2019, with 335 out of 384 days (87.2%) monitored. Pelagic thresher sharks were present on 120 of these days (35.8% of total days monitored) with a total of 211 thresher shark encounters determined over the study period. The study found that 43.6% of thresher shark encounters took place in the late morning, and seasonal peak was observed during the cool dry months of the Amihan season (52.1% of encounters were recorded between December and February). Willage and Thandy’s Rocks were identified as the two dive sites within Manta Bowl most visited by these sharks. Despite the listing of pelagic thresher sharks in the CITES appendix II in 2016 and its implementation in 2017, both targeted and non-targeted catch of the species continues unmonitored and unmanaged. In the nearby Donsol market, we found 94 landed individuals between January 29 and March 19, 2020. Considering the declaration of the protected status of the TBPPS in 2018, this seamount represents a key habitat for the conservation of this species. As such, fishery management interventions including delineation of no-fishing areas, restrictions on non-selective fishing gear, and landing monitoring are urgently needed.

5865: The Dreketi River, on Fiji’s second largest island Vanua Levu, is considered the deepest river in Fiji and one of the few remaining rivers in Fiji that has not yet been dredged. The Dreketi Estuary spans a width of approximately 7km and extends 3km to the seaward margins with an alluvial fan that covers 15km2. Sampling sites were established across the estuary and up to 18km upriver. Fishery-independent survey undertaken over a period of 20 days, comprised of 75 hours of gill net soak time, yielded a total of 85 elasmobranch captures and a total elasmobranch catch per unit effort (CPUE) of 1.13 captures per hour. Of the total captures there were 4 species of shark; 47 scalloped hammerhead sharks (55%), 14 blacktip sharks (16%), 8 great hammerhead sharks (9%) and 8 bull sharks (9%) and 3 species of ray; 6 ocellated eagle rays (7%), 1 pink whipray (1%) and 1 bottlenose wedgefish (1%). The high proportion of sharks with either a healed or semi-healed umbilical scar indicates parturition and early life residency in the Dreketi Estuary and River and spatial data indicates a degree of species segregation with different species tending to utilize or remain in distinct areas within the study site. Based on anecdotal information the area is known to have a higher concentration of sharks than surrounding coastal areas and the presence of juvenile sharks has been an annual occurrence for many years. Elasmobranchs have been noted to have a geospatial affinity to certain areas that can allow the species increased access for food and protection. The identification of such areas can be particularly vital for migratory species such as the scalloped hammerhead shark, the great hammerhead shark and the bull shark which are intrinsically difficult to manage and may warrant marine protected area status.

5866: Accurate species delineation is integral to many aspects of theoretical biology as well as applied natural resource management. However, discriminating species can be problematic, particularly for species that have recently diverged and/or are very similar morphologically. Species concepts vary and no one definition works for all taxonomic groups, nor does anyone tool. Next generation sequencing technologies are providing greater resolution in DNA markers to address species discrimination studies, particularly for non-model organisms. Here we present on two studies that examine cryptic species in chondrichthyan fishes: devil rays (Mobula spp.) and bamboo sharks (Chiloscyllium spp.). We examine and compare genetic differences within genera between mitochondrial DNA sequence data and genomic data generated from genotyping by sequencing (DArTSeq). We find that genomic data provide greater resolution to discriminate between species compared with mitochondrial DNA. We discuss the challenges for interpreting the results including how the greater resolution provided by genomic data compared with genetic data may lead to over-splitting and speciesinflation, particularly for geographically separated groups. 5867: Galapagos sharks, Carcharhinus galapagensis, are abundant at Lord Howe Island and regularly interact with fishing gear, leading to bycatch and depredation. This causes negative impacts for the fishers through lost bait, fishing gear and catch, as well as for the sharks due to altered natural behaviour, hook injuries or death due to deliberate killing. To understand this sharkfisher conflict and identify ways to mitigate it, we have been using a combined approach including acoustic telemetry, vessel tracking, logbook data and surveys of local fisher knowledge. Galapagos sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and detected within a receiver array across depths from 15–75m and charter fishing vessel activity was determined using Vessel Monitoring Systemdata. Kernel density analyses assessed the spatial and temporal overlap between shark detections and fishing vessel presence, identifying several areas where higher fishing effort overlapped with greater shark detections, predominantly at shelf edges. Substantially higher residency values were recorded for three individuals tagged at a location where fish waste is regularly discarded, potentially indicating a change in behaviour and movement patterns resulting from regular food provision. Statistical models indicated that detection rates were higher in locations with higher fishing activity, greater bathymetric complexity and during summer. Logbook data showed a mean annual catch of 1,114 sharks with >95% released. Fishers reported methods that they currently use to reduce shark interactions, including fishing deeper than 150m, switching from rod and reel to handlines and electric reels, using jigs and lures instead of bait and rotating fishing locations so as not to regularly return to the same sites. Diversifying target species also helped to minimise shark interactions. The holistic combination of approaches used in this study has provided detailed insights into the shark-fisher conflict occurring at Lord Howe Island and identified key strategies to reduce these negative interactions.

5868: The sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus) has a global distribution and is caught by commercial and recreational fishers. We assessed the post-release survival of sandbar sharks caught in longline surveys conducted in Western Australia (WA) using an integrated approach that combined the use of hook-timers, release condition staging, satellite tagging, and blood physiology (adrenocorticotropic hormone, corticosterone, and lactate). Of the 57 individuals examined, 88% were “alive and strong” with 100% initial survival when released after a maximum of four hours on the hook. Of the 13 satellite-tagged individuals, 100% survived. Sharks dived up to 307 m deep and showed cyclical depth movement patterns with some individuals moving up and down the water column both day and night, while others moved almost exclusively at night, corresponding with the movement patterns of squid, a common prey item of sandbar sharks. The concentration of blood metabolites did not show a linear pattern with time on hook. The 100% survival rate within four hours on the hooks suggests the use of longlines for surveying sandbar shark abundance has no deleterious consequences.

5869: Mesh net fisheries face challenges in reducing bycatch, especially when interacting with species of conservation interest (SOCI) such as dugongs and hammerhead sharks in iconic locations such as the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area (GBRWHA). In this region, bycatch mortality of both SOCI and of undersized or unwanted fishes has severely affected the fishery's social license and has exacerbated conflict, especially with recreational fishers. However, tunnel net gears can help to address bycatch mortality issues. These gears are essentially large, mobile fish traps where the catch is guided into a submerged tunnel where it remains free-swimming until brailling and sorting where bycatch is released in very good condition. Larger species including elasmobranchs such as hammerheads and wedgefishes, and stingrays are prevented from entering the tunnel by large mesh grids, and remain free swimming in a holding area until release. Increasing regulatory pressure and public scrutiny of net fisheries in the GBRWHA are driving efforts to find innovative solutions to improve sustainability and community support for fisheries while maintaining fisher livelihoods. This presentation will describe the results of a small-scale feasibility trial of the use of tunnel net gears in the shallow coastal waters of the Great Barrier Reef. Funded by the FRDC, expert tunnel net fishers worked with local inshore net fishers to trial and test the use of tunnel nets in the northern GBRWHA. The factors affecting the suitability and feasibility of using these gears will be discussed, as well as resulting catch composition and volume, estimated immediate bycatch mortality, and accounts of SOCI interactions. The perspectives and attitudes of commercial fishers and other stakeholders engaged during the trials will also be presented.

5870: The Kimberley Marine Park spans a 74,469 km2 area off the coast of north-western Australia and represents a biologically important refuge for marine megafauna, notably humpback whales, dolphins, dugongs, and turtles, amidst extensive coral communities. Despite this, there is very little information available on demersal shark diversity and population estimates across this vast marine park. In this study, we directly compared the efficacy of eDNA metabarcoding and conventional longline deployments to survey demersal and pelagic elasmobranchs in the Kimberley Marine Park and more broadly. Seawater samples were collected for eDNA screening within 12 hours post-longline deployment at 36 sites across a 55,000 square-kilometre area. In total, we recovered 50 elasmobranch taxa, 36 of which were detected by eDNA and 32 (from a total of 815 captured sharks) by longline; a combined approach yielding over 38% more elasmobranch taxa than either approach alone. Site community compositions notably varied between the two survey approaches, but also from broader environmental influences, such as depth and latitude. We additionally investigate whether eDNA metabarcoding read abundance data correlates with longline aggregate catch data and assess required levels of eDNA replication and longline deployments to maximise captured elasmobranch diversity, whilst minimising longline fatalities. This study sets an integrated baseline and long-term monitoring approach for the management and conservation of elasmobranch diversity within this unique marine park.

5871: There are increasing concerns over the possible impacts of aquaculture pens on the local abundance and residency of sharks, and its associated risk for shark bites at nearby beaches and surf breaks. We used acoustic tracking and a before-during-after-control-impact (BACI) design to assess the residency and local abundance of 117 bronze whalers and >1,000 white sharks around a 45m diameter aquaculture pen installed in South Australia for tourism purposes. Only 14 bronze whalers and nine white sharks were detected throughout the fiveyear monitoring period. There was no clear evidence of the pen attracting bronze whalers or white sharks, in either the number of sharks detected or number of detections (proxy for length of time detected). While previous studies and reports indicate that the aquaculture industry can affect shark behaviour and residency patterns, our study shows that the aquaculture pen used for tourism off South Australia did not lead to an increased number of sharks nor increased residency of sharks in its vicinity. The low amount of interactions with the pen was likely due to a combination of factors: low fish biomass, pen installed in a shallow location, local shark species being migratory species, and good husbandry practices. Understanding the factors leading to changes in shark behaviour and movement patterns is complex and will require further studies across several aquaculture industries, ideally using a BACI design similar to that used in this study.

5872: Wildlife tourism is expanding around the world, and so is the need to quantify its possible detrimental effects on the very species it targets. To date, studies on the effects of tourism on marine organisms have focused almost exclusively on documenting behavioural changes, but whether such changes affect the energy budgets, demography, and ultimately, the survival prospects of the targeted animals is mostly unknown. This lack of knowledge is particularly acute for large, predatory sharks that are difficult to study but economically important. Animal-borne cameras and accelerometer loggers were deployed on 20 white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) recording 489.7 hours (20.4 days) of data to assess white shark behaviour and activity when interacting with cage-diving vessels at the Neptune Islands Group Marine Park, South Australia. A random forest machine learning algorithm was used to predict white shark behaviours based on 62 hours of known behavioural acceleration signals. The presence of cage-diving vessels increased the amount of time spent performing high energy behaviours such as high activity swimming (vectorial dynamic body acceleration [VeDBA] 0.04 ± 0.03 g; three-fold increase) and bursts of acceleration (veDBA 0.44 ± 0.38 g; ten-fold increase) while halving low activity swimming (veDBA 0.021 ± 0.013 g). However, once put in the context of daily energy budget and accounting for the duration of cage-diving activities (~4 hours per day), white shark energy expenditure was not substantially affected by cage-diving tourism. Our study shows that changes in shark activity due to wildlife tourism does not necessarily lead to a negative impact on the energy expenditure of individual sharks. 5873: Researchers studying animals need to ensure that sampling procedures and the methods they use are as harmless and non-disruptive as possible, particularly when their focal species are threatened or protected. White sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) are Vulnerable and protected globally, and are frequently studied by marine ecologists. Here we assessed white shark responses to research activities (i.e. tagging and biopsy procedures, and electric deterrent trials) conducted at the Neptune Islands Group Marine Park (South Australia, Australia). Trends in shark residency following the research activities were assessed and shark abundance (number of sharks detected and sighted by cage-diving operators) were compared before, during, and after scientific expeditions, and to natural fluctuations in the absence of research activities using eight years (2013–2021) of acoustic tracking and daily sighting reports from a wildlife tourism industry. White shark residency decreased through time but was not affected by sampling (tagging and biopsying). Shark abundance declined following sampling and deterrent trials, but the rates of decline were similar to natural fluctuations in shark abundance. Our study shows that external tagging, biopsies, or deterrent trials do not affect short- and long-term residency or abundance of white sharks, probably due to their strong immune systems and remarkable ability to heal from injuries. Re-evaluating study methods forms part of the researcher’s responsibilities to ensure best practice and abide by national and international codes for the care and use of animals for scientific purposes. 5874: Elasmobranchs are among the world’s most threatened vertebrate families, due in part to their reliance on coastal ecosystems that are disproportionately affected by urbanisation, habitat loss, and climate change. Shoreline environments provide elasmobranchs with vital shelter and prey items, but are also more susceptible to environmental (e.g. temperature, waves, freshwater input) and anthropogenic (wastewater, pollution) changes than pelagic ecosystems. Our study will quantify and compare the relationship between space use and diet of benthic and pelagic elasmobranchs in Australia and identify the impacts of urbanisation. Specifically, this study aims to 1) consolidate the methods used to prepare tissues for biochemical analysis (fatty acid and stable isotope analysis) and 2) develop isotopic diet-tissue discrimination factors and fatty acid calibration coefficients for sharks and rays. These methods will then be combined with acoustic tracking techniques to 3) quantify the trophic and spatial niche of sharks and rays in a coastal, benthic environment (Gulf St Vincent) and 4) a pelagic environment (Norfolk Island) to determine the relationship between space use and trophic ecology and assess how this is affected across species ecology and levels of urbanisation. The results from this study will improve upon biochemical methods used in trophic ecology studies, demonstrate the use of these methods on elasmobranchs in different environments and levels of urbanisation, and determine the relationship between trophic and spatial ecology. These results will be valuable for determining the extent to which elasmobranchs may be impacted by anthropogenic pressure and whether certain ocean activities require mitigation to reduce their impacts. 5875: Located ~600km offshore from the New South Wales coast, the State and Commonwealth marine parks surrounding Lord Howe Island support the world’s most southerly coral reef, are renowned for their biodiversity, and offer unique opportunities for tourism and recreational activities, including fishing. The Galapagos shark (Carcharhinus galapagensis) is the most common shark species in these World Heritage Listed marine parks. Yet, their regular interaction with fishing vessels in the area, where they consume bait and hooked fish (depredation), has negative impacts on both the local charter fishing industry and the sharks themselves (through altered natural behaviours, injuries, and targeted killing). Because of these impacts, the negative interactions between sharks and fishers pose a threat to a range of social, economic, and environmental values within the parks. A multi-year project is underway to improve our understanding of recurring depredation events in the marine parks. We are using a holistic approach that utilises data from: acoustic telemetry and a Vessel Monitoring System to assess the overlap between fishing effort and shark movement patterns; a social survey to investigate the perception of the local community towards this shark species; Baited Remote Underwater Video surveys to quantify shark abundance in fished and non-fished areas; the NSW gamefish tagging program to estimate shark re-capture rates and movements; and fishery logbook reports (paper-based and electronic) to determine depredation rates and associated financial loss (gear and catch). Genetic samples have also been collected from >70 individual sharks to assess the effective population size and structure in the marine parks, as well as population connectivity to other areas in the southwest Pacific, using Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms. Together, these results will be compiled into a conceptual environmental management model that integrates the different ecological, social and economic aspects, to help us identify optimal management scenarios that benefit both sharks and the local community. Knowledge from this research will allow us to understand the factors influencing shark depredation interactions, recommend potential solutions and management strategies to reduce negative interactions between sharks and fishers, and therefore enhance a range of values for both marine parks. 5876: The Maugean skate, Zearaja maugeana, is endemic to two isolated western Tasmanian (Australia) estuaries. The species' persistence in one of these estuaries (Bathurst Harbour) is uncertain, while the other estuary (Macquarie Harbour), potentially the remaining stronghold for the species, is an anthropogenically impacted system. The species has been recently (2021) included as one of the nine finfish top priority species within the Threatened Species Strategy List by the Department of Agriculture, Water and Environment (Australia Government). Key life-history parameters, ageing and reproduction, were studied to inform conservation actions for this species. Reproductive information was obtained using non-lethal methodologies, circulating concentrations of sex steroids and ultrasonography. Growth and age parameters were estimated based on vertebral sections from a small sample of individuals. Females and males reached 870- and 760-mm total length, respectively. The species reached a maximum age of at least 10 years. Females and males attained 50% sexual maturity at 665- and 633-mm total length, respectively, probably maturing somewhere between four and six years of age. Females displayed an asynchronous, discontinuous reproductive cycle, being able to reproduce throughout the year, with a probable decline in reproductive activity during summer. No egg cases were observed in-utero. Males produce sperm all year round, with a peak in testosterone production during spring–autumn. Conservation strategies for Z. maugeana will need to focus on reducing anthropogenic impacts on the environmental health of Macquarie Harbour. Currently, there is a continuous work to better understand how reproductive success, egg survival and recruitment are affected by these environmental challenges.

5877: Biological rhythms that are mediated by exogenous factors, such as light and temperature, drive the physiology of organisms and affect processes ranging from cellular to population levels. For elasmobranchs (shark, rays, and skates), studies documenting diel activity and movement patterns indicate that many species are crepuscular or nocturnal in nature. However, few studies have investigated the rhythmicity of elasmobranch physiology to understand the mechanisms underpinning these distinct patterns. Here, we assess diel patterns of metabolic rates in a small meso-predator, the epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), across ecologically relevant temperatures and upon acutely removing photoperiod cues. This species, like other buccal pumping, benthic elasmobranchs, uses behavioural sleep, which is reflected herein by low metabolic rates during the day and 1.7fold increases in metabolic rates at night. From spring to summer seasons, where average temperatures for this species range from 24.5 to 28.5°C, time of day, and not temperature, had the strongest influence on metabolic rate. These results may indicate that this species, and perhaps other similar tropical or demersal species, have physiological mechanisms in place to maintain metabolic rate regardless of temperature fluctuations that are relevant to their native habitats.

5878: Norfolk Island is a small island in the Pacific Ocean, ~1,400 km east of Australia that supports a broad diversity of temperate and tropical marine life, including many shark and pelagic fish species. In particular, Norfolk Island is home to a large aggregation of mature female tiger sharks Galeocerdo cuvier, with unknown diet, foraging ecology, and movement patterns. While the reliability of this aggregation makes Norfolk Island an ideal site to uncover the ecology of these top predators, no work to date has quantitatively explored what tiger sharks consume in this region, or how long they spend in these coastal waters. The local community has also raised concerns about the disposal of cow offal, rubbish, and fish frames, which are presumed to attract the tiger sharks that are observed feeding at the disposal sight. Here, we used stable isotopes and fatty acids from 60 tiger shark blood and muscle samples collected in 2020 and 2021 to quantify the role of cow offal in the diet of these generalist predators. Despite the frequent observation of tiger sharks consuming cow offal, isotope models suggest that local seabirds are the predominate prey source for these large tiger sharks sampled around Norfolk Island.

5879: River sharks (Glyphis spp.) and some sawfishes (Pristidae) inhabit riverine environments, but their long-term habitat use patterns in rivers are poorly known. We investigated the diadromous movements of the northern river shark (Glyphis garricki), speartooth shark (Glyphis glyphis), narrow sawfish (Anoxypristis cuspidata), and the largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) using laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) on vertebrae to recover elemental ratios over an individual’s lifetime. We also measured elemental ratios for the bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas) and a range of inshore and offshore stenohaline marine species to assist in interpretation of results. Ba was found to be an effective indicator of freshwater, while Sr and Li were effective indicators of marine water. The relationship between Ba and Sr was consistently inverse. Both river shark species had prolonged use of upper estuarine environments, while adults appear to mainly use lower estuarine environments rather than marine. In comparison, a wide range of freshwater, estuarine, and marine environments were observed for C. leucas. For P. pristis, decreases in Sr : Ba at the end of the pre-natal growth zone indicated that parturition likely occurs in freshwater. There was limited evidence of prolonged riverine habitat use for A. cuspidata. The results of this study support elemental-environment relationships observed in teleost otoliths are also applicable to a wide range of elasmobranch species. A greater understanding of processes that lead to element incorporation in vertebrae, and relative concentrations in vertebrae with respect to the ambient environment, will improve the applicability of elemental analysis to inform life history movements of elasmobranchs into the future. 5880: The characterisation of predator-prey interactions and trophic role within marine food webs are essential to understand community dynamics and to enable ecosystem-based management. In particular, the functions of mesopredators as ecologically-important trophic links are often overlooked in favour of primary producers or top predators. Elephant fish (Callorhinchus milii) are presumed to be a regionally-important mesopredator across southern Australia and New Zealand, yet little is known about the fundamental biology and ecology of the species. Diet comparisons from two Australian locations and one New Zealand location enabled the assessment of spatial variations in feeding ecology and trophic niche across different spatial scales. Our findings improve our understanding of elephant fish trophic ecology, and chimaera ecology more broadly, for which minimal information is currently available.

5881: Due to their large size, slow growth and late maturity, skates are some of the most vulnerable exploited marine fish species. The Melbourne skate (Spiniraja whitleyi), a large skate endemic to the continental shelf of Australia, has experienced significant declines in local abundance, a trend attributed to sustained trawling activity. Due to the Melbourne skate’s vulnerability to local extinction, the collection of scientific data directly relevant to conservation of the species is now a matter of urgency. My PhD aims to address this information gap by providing baseline data to steer effective fisheries and conservation management efforts for this vulnerable species. 5882: Patterns of genetic connectivity can be used to define the geographic boundaries of fishes and underpin management decisions. This study used a genetic multi-marker approach to investigate the population structure of scalloped hammerheads (Sphyrna lewini) in the Indo– Pacific. Samples from 541 S. lewini were collected from 12 locations across the Indo–Pacific. Samples were analysed using two regions of the mitochondrial genome, nine microsatellite loci and two sets of Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNP). Our study has four key findings; (1) genetic structure of S. lewini across the Indo–Pacific is affected by oceanic basins and can be separated into four distinct regions. (2) Within the central Indo–Pacific, connectivity is facilitated along continental shelves and strong signals of Isolation-By-Distance (IBD) were observed. (3) Mitochondrial haplotypes previously thought only to exist in the Atlantic Ocean are observed in Indo–Pacific populations, suggesting the haplotype should be reconsidered as more widespread than initially thought. (4) Results from microsatellites and SNPs largely agree, however a few differences are apparent with SNPs identifying more discrete population subdivision. Our findings suggest management at the spatial scales and boundaries identified in this study will necessitate international and national cooperation to conserve S. lewini populations.

5883: The scale and drivers of marine biodiversity loss are being revealed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List assessment process. We present the first global reassessment of 1,199 species in Class Chondrichthyes – sharks, rays, and chimaeras. The first global assessment (in 2014) concluded that one-quarter (24%) of species were threatened. Now, 391 (32.6%) species are threatened with extinction. When this percentage of threat is applied to Data Deficient species, more than one-third (37.5%) of chondrichthyans are estimated to be threatened, with much of this change resulting from new information. Three species are Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct), representing possibly the first global marine fish extinctions due to overfishing. Consequently, the chondrichthyan extinction rate is potentially 25 extinctions per million species years, comparable to that of terrestrial vertebrates. Overfishing is the universal threat affecting all 391 threatened species and is the sole threat for 67.3% of species and interacts with three other threats for the remaining third: loss and degradation of habitat (31.2% of threatened species), climate change (10.2%), and pollution (6.9%). Species are disproportionately threatened in tropical and subtropical coastal waters. Science-based limits on fishing, effective marine protected areas, and approaches that reduce or eliminate fishing mortality are urgently needed to minimise mortality of threatened species and ensure sustainable catch and trade of others. Immediate action is essential to prevent further extinctions and protect the potential for food security and ecosystem functions provided by this iconic lineage of predators.

5884: Knowledge of the three-dimensional movement patterns of elasmobranchs is vital to understanding their ecological roles and exposure to anthropogenic pressures. To date, comparative studies among species at global scales have mostly focused on horizontal movements. Our study addresses the knowledge gap of vertical movements by compiling the first global synthesis of vertical habitat use by elasmobranchs from data obtained by deployment of 989 biotelemetry tags on 38 elasmobranch species. Elasmobranchs displayed high intra- and interspecific variability in vertical movement patterns across both geographical and diel scales, highlighting the complex behaviours adopted by this diverse taxonomic group. Yet, significant vertical overlap was observed for many epipelagic elasmobranchs, indicating an increased likelihood to display spatial overlap, biologically interact, and share similar risk to anthropogenic threats that vary on a vertical gradient. We highlight the critical next steps towards incorporating vertical movement into global management and monitoring strategies for elasmobranchs, emphasising the need to address geographic and taxonomic biases in deployments and to concurrently consider both horizontal and vertical movements. 5885: Fisheries management is essential to guarantee sustainable capture of target species, and to avoid undesirable impacts on incidentally caught species. A key challenge is to assess the status of species and the degree to which management is sufficient to avoid declines in relatively data-poor fisheries. While ecological risk analyses focus on intrinsic ‘productivity’ and extrinsic ‘susceptibility’, one would ideally understand the third axis of ‘fisheries management’. Currently, there is no single management evaluation that can be applied to a range of data-poor fishery types. Here, we outline a management risk (M-Risk) framework for sharks, rays, and chimaeras that can be used to evaluate a species’ risk to overfishing resulting from ineffective management. We illustrate our approach with application to one country (Ecuador) and one regional fisheries management organisation (RFMO) (Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission) and show the variation in scores between species. We found that while both management units assessed had similar overall scores, the scores for individual attributes varied. Ecuador scored higher in reporting-related attributes, while the RFMO scored higher in attributes related to data collection and its use. We evaluated whether management of individual species was sufficient for their relative sensitivity by the combining the management risk score for each species with their intrinsic sensitivity to determine a final overall M-Risk score. This framework can be applied to determine which species face the greatest risk of overfishing and be used by fisheries managers to identify effective management policies by replicating regulations from countries with lower risk scores.

5887: The presence of predators can elicit anti-predatory behaviors in prey, which have the capacity to affect their fitness (risk effects) and can cause cascading impacts to lower trophic levels. In coral reef systems, the anti-predatory responses of reef fishes are difficult to observe as the presence of a diver may be regarded as a threat by prey fishes, confounding responses to predators such as sharks. To overcome this issue, we used an animated, life-size model of a blacktip reef shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus) to simulate predatory threat to mesopredatory reef fishes (MRF; e.g. lutjanids). The responses of the MRF to the model were compared to those generated by three non- threatening controls (life-size model of a turtle, PVC-pipe and Perspex shape). Additionally, a snorkeler provided a second threat treatment. A Remote Underwater Stereo-Video System recorded the approach of the treatments and allowed us to measure Flight Initiation Distance (FID) and categorize the type of flight response by fishes. We found that MRF had greater FIDs in response to the approaching threatening models (1402 ± 167 - 1533 ± 171 mm) compared to the controls (706 ± 151 - 896 ± 163 mm). There was no significant difference in FID of MRF between the shark model and the snorkeler, suggesting that these treatments provoked similar levels of anti-predator behavior. The most frequent type of reaction was flight (shark: 64.3%, snorkeler: 52%, controls: 37% - 16.1%), followed by retreat into a crevice (shark: 14.2%, snorkeler: 28%, controls: 11.1% - 9.7%). Our study suggests that, irrespective of the degree to which sharks consume MRF, they still elicit a predictable and consistent anti-predator response. The presence of a snorkeler evoked the same anti-predator response, which has implications for both prey species in terms of risk effects and for researchers using underwater census and monitoring behavior in situ.

5888: In the 2019/20 fishing year, Antarctic starry skates (Amblyraja georgiana) were tagged with the antibiotic terramycin (oxytetracycline hydrochloride, OTC) or strontium chloride for a mark-recapture programme established to estimate population size and validate caudal thorn ageing techniques. More than 2,100 skates were injected of the 4,900 tagged (42%). During the 2019/20 and 2020/21 fishing seasons, a total of 49 skates were recaptured and retained and samples from 28 skates were available for analysis at this time. Six of the recaptured skates returned were injected with OTC and one skate was injected with strontium chloride according to observer records (25% of returned samples analysed). Two samples at liberty for at least one year had good edge fluorescence, which may be indicative of OTC uptake in the caudal thorns. However, further examination of the vertebrae of these two skates also showed edge fluorescence, and this is suspected to be a result of auto-fluorescence due to a residual skirt of integument. Further sampling is required to determine if age validation can be assessed with caudal thorns. Continued sampling of recaptured skates is currently ongoing to increase the sample size of OTC-injected skates. No recording.

5889: Delineation of population structure (i.e. stocks) is crucial for successfully manage of exploited species and to address conservation concerns for threatened species. Migration and associated movements are key mechanisms through which discrete populations mix and are thus important determinants of population structure. Detailed information on migration and movements is becoming more accessible through advances in telemetry and analysis methods; however, such information is not yet used systematically in stock structure assessment. Here, we described how detections of acoustically tagged sharks across a continental-scale array of underwater acoustic receivers were used to assess stock structure and connectivity in seven species and compared to findings from genetic and conventional tagging. Network analysis revealed previously unknown population connections in some species, and in others bolstered support for existing stock discrimination by identifying nodes and routes important for connectivity. Species with less variability in their movements required smaller sample sizes (45–50 individuals) to reveal useful stock structure information. Our study shows the power of continental-scale acoustic telemetry networks to detect movements among management jurisdictions. We highlight methodological issues that need to be considered in the design of acoustic telemetry studies for investigating stock structure and the interpretation of the resulting data. The advent of broad-scale acoustic telemetry networks across the globe provides new avenues to understand how movement informs population structure and can lead to improved management.

5890: Like other species of marine megafauna, sharks and rays have economic, cultural and spiritual value to the people of the Pacific Islands. The cultural and traditional importance of sharks and rays is demonstrated in Pacific stories, legends, customs, artifacts, chants/calling as well as traditional tattoo designs and weapons. Sharks and rays are also an important protein source that has sustained many Pacific communities for generations. Traditional fishing methods used by ancestors to catch sharks to feed families and their communities are still in use in some communities in the Pacific. Traditionally, people took only what was needed for their community and families, thus ensuring that marine resources would be available to them in the future. As the populations of many shark species have declined, primarily through industrial scale fishing, Pacific island countries have demonstrated global leadership as strong advocates of promoting shark conservation and management at global and international forums. Pacific countries have established shark sanctuaries prohibiting the commercial fishing, sale and trade of sharks and rays within their Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). As a result, shark and ray tourism has been rapidly expanding in some Pacific countries. Other countries have put in place protected areas for critical nursery habitats for vulnerable shark and ray species. This presentation will highlight some of these efforts and how the Pacific are stepping up to strengthen conservation measures for these species. 5980: The earliest Chondrichthyes appeared 400 million years ago and have maintained their overall body shape essentially unchanged since their origins. This long evolutionary history has brought them to develop body and fin characteristics and an efficient swimming mode that allow them to occupy different habitats successfully. According to recent hydrodynamics studies, compared to the other fins, the tail is the one that plays a crucial role in overall locomotor functions and its shape appears to be correlated with the habitat occupied by the shark. Previous works have investigated this correlation analysing museum specimens or scientific illustrations, while those that have focused on live animals were able to study only few individuals of few species. Using photos taken from freshly fished sharks here, we investigated the diversity of the form of caudal fins in 37 species belonging to 3 orders to verify the relationships between the variability of shape and occupied habitat. Geometric morphometric analysis was used to study the shape of the tail through the positioning of 5 landmarks. Moreover, the aspect ratios of the caudal fins were calculated. Information regarding the habitat and bathymetric range occupied by each species was obtained from scientific database. Relations between the occupied habitat and caudal fin shape were investigated taking into account phylogenetic relationships. This study contributes to the understanding of the relation between morphology and ecology in the light of the evolution of sharks.

5981: A number of different models have been developed to describe growth (e.g., von Bertalanffy, Gompertz, Logistic), however no single growth model provides the best fit for describing a population growth. This study presents the results obtained by fitting a biphasic growth model to describe lifetime growth of Scyliorhinus canicula population in the Cantabrian Sea (NE Atlantic). Data used for all these models was based on tag-recapture database updated from a tagging program conducted in the study area since 1993. A total of 14091 lesser spotted dogfish have been tagged during this period, 7638 males and 6453 females respectively from which 496 were recaptured. Parameters obtained from Lester growth model (LGM) provided a juvenile annual growth rate (h= 57.4 ±1.2 mm) and reproductive investment (g~ 0.20). Besides, after conversion, the following von Bertalanffy growth parameters (VBGC), for sexes combined, valid only for post reproductory lifetime, were: Linf=84.5 cm; k=0.083, t0=-2.25. Growth models (VB), such as Gompertz or logistic were compared and differences were discussed taking into account both life history traits and fishing pressure acting on the population studied. Finally mortality estimates (M) based on previous growth models were calculated. Parameters derived from growth models are used to estimate important life history traits.
5982: Sharks, rays, and skates - the elasmobranchii - are currently not known to actively produce sounds in the wild. Here, we present multiple records of voluntary sound production in the wild, by two species of stingray, namely the mangrove whipray Urogymnus granulatus and the cowtail stingray Pastinachus ater. Sounds recorded from both species are characterised by a series of very short and loud clicks and appear to serve the purpose of agonistic displays. In all recorded observations, a ray commenced producing sounds in response to an observer approaching closely, and ceased sound production when the distance between the ray and observer increased. Our study illustrates that elasmobranchs can produce sounds, and that more research into this ability is required.

5983: Among the numerous aquatic species displayed in aquaria worldwide, chimaeroid fishes play a special role. Not only these scarce and delicate species are very attractive to the visitor’s education but they still have unsuspected ecological adaptations to deep-sea environments. Knowledge of these adaptations and life traits of deep-sea species are key elements to their conservation, even for species that are not directly endangered by anthropic activities. The basic nutritional and environmental needs of spotted ratfish (Hydrolagus colliei) are known, however, husbandry and breeding of this species still require crucial information to be successfully achieved. Successful breeding was first reported in Japan in early 2000 with barely one year of survival. In Europe, the EUAC Ratfish Monitoring Program reported mating behaviors between captive H. colliei specimens as well as egg-laying for more than two decades. However, few hatchings only were reported between 2008 and 2015, with subsequent poor survival rates. Since 2018, Planet Ocean Montpellier (POM, France) aquarists observed an increased number of egg cases in tanks, inducing a greater number of hatchings in 2019. To date, the oldest H. colliei specimens born in captivity at POM are more than three years old. Since 2019, egg cases and juveniles are closely monitored and embryonic development is regularly recorded. This presentation will focus on H. colliei husbandry and breeding at POM, in an attempt to reconcile observations from aquarists and research. It will include environmental and developmental data that have been collected for 16 years on embryos, juveniles, and mature specimens.

5984: The Angelshark (Squatina squatina) is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN and the Spanish Catalogue of Endangered Species. It has suffered a decline across Europe of at least 80% during the last century, mainly attributed to overfishing and habitat degradation. However, a uniquely large stronghold for this species remains in an island archipelago in the middle of the East Atlantic Ocean – the Canary Islands. In the Canary Islands this species has an idyllic place to develop its life cycle, with no trawling or directed fishing activity, a variety of environmental conditions and abundant prey. A key part of their life cycle occurs in nursery areas, where the offspring are born and spend their first life stages. Since 2015, the Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) has conducted different studies focused in these areas, designed to assess nursery are criteria established by Heupel et al. 2007. ASP:CI have then developed a point-based mechanism to compare different sites and identify those that are confirmed, potential and possible nursery areas. To date, ASP:CI have discovered seven confirmed nursery areas, six potential nursery areas and 42 sites where juveniles are present but need further study. Further, this talk will describe some of the environmental and biological drivers of juvenile Angel shark distribution across the archipelago. ASP:CI nursery area research was funded by Shark Conservation Fund, Disney Conservation Fund, Save our Seas Foundation, The Biodiversity Consultancy, BIAZA, German Elasmobranch Group and WWF Netherlands.

5985: Rhino rays or wedgefishes (Rhynchobatus spp) are threatened by illegal trade globally and in the Southwest Indian Ocean (SWIO) due to their high-value fins on the international shark-fin market. Rhynchobatus australiae and Rhynchobatus djiddensis are classified as Critically Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, yet little is known about the distribution of genetic diversity and populations across the SWIO region. This hinders assessments of population trends that are required for effective conservation strategies. Previous molecular species identification confirmed all samples from South Africa and Mozambique to be R. djiddensis while those from Madagascar, Tanzania and Seychelles were identified as R. australiae. Here we investigated the genetic diversity and connectivity within and between species and sampling locations using sequence data from three mitochondrial gene regions (cytochrome oxidase I, nicotinamide adenine dehydrogenase subunit 2, mitochondrial control region) and 9 nuclear microsatellite markers developed from high-throughput sequencing data. We also developed molecular resources to aid in accurate species identification and subsequent genetic analysis, including complete annotated mitogenomes of R. djiddensis and R. australiae and optimized eDNA (environmental DNA) metabarcoding assays based on the 12S and 16S ribosomal RNA gene regions. This knowledge could further the genetic characterization of populations of these and related species and promote the taxonomic resolution of the Rhynchobatus species complex.

5986: The Canary Islands have been identified as a unique stronghold for the Angelshark, Squatina squatina, because it can be seen relatively frequently by divers and fishers. The species is highly susceptible to accidental capture in fisheries and habitat degradation, due to its benthic ecology and coastal location. This has caused the species to be listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, and action is required for its protection. In 2019, Angelsharks were listed in the Spanish Endangered Species List for Canary Islands waters, under “In danger of extinction” (highest category within this legislation). In accordance with this listing, it was required that a Recovery Plan be developed, including appropriate measures for the management and conservation of Angelsharks. Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) ran a series of in-person and online surveys to collate information on Angelshark interactions, perceptions and possible measures to improve their protection with three main user groups: divers, recreational fishers and commercial fishers. This information was used alongside ASP:CI scientific data and a collaborative workshop with stakeholder representatives to identify the location of conservation areas and co-design specific conservation measures in order to safeguard the future of Angelsharks in their uniquely large stronghold. This presentation will outline our key findings and the importance of using a participatory approach to design conservation measures for a Critically Endangered species. This work, led by ASP:CI, was funded by Shark Conservation Fund and through a contract with the Canary Islands Government, co-financed by the FEDER 2014-2020 Operational Program.

5987: Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) is a broad-spectrum pesticide banned in Brazil since 1998. One of its main metabolites, dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene (DDE), is highly persistent, fat-soluble and extremely toxic to aquatic organisms. Scarce studies in elasmobranchs are available, and none have been performed for the Brazilian guitarfish Pseudobatos horkelii. Herein, DDE concentrations were determined in the livers of 22 Brazilian guitarfish individuals, five non-pregnant adult females, two pregnant females, 10 embryos (eight females, two males) and five adult males and correlated to the hepatosomatic index (HSI), gonadosomatic index (GSI) and condition factor (CF) for all groups. Maternal transfer was confirmed, as embryos contained detectable amounts of DDE, albeit lower than in all adult groups. Higher concentrations were found in adult males compared to non-pregnant adult females and embryos, and intermediate values were observed for adult pregnant females. The higher values observed in males may reflect the maternal contaminant offloading processes through female ovulation and pregnancy processes, resulting in lower DDE concentrations, as noted for other elasmobranchs. The positive correlations noted between DDE and the IHS and negative correlations between DDE concentrations and the IGS for all groups (including embryos) indicate potentially deleterious systemic health effects for the liver and reproductive systems, respectively, beginning in the womb and indicating serious concerns for the species. Finally, negative correlations between DDE concentrations and the FC indicate that this pesticide metabolite may result in potential general health effects. This is the first study to assess DDE concentrations and maternal offloading processes in this Critically Endangered species.

5988: Sawsharks are demersal sharks characterised by a distinctive saw-like rostrum with a pair of long barbels on the ventral surface. In Australia, two sawshark species – the common (Pristiophorus cirratus) and southern (P. nudipinnis) sawshark – are frequent by-catch in commercial fisheries and sold for human consumption. Although harvesting is currently considered sustainable, much of the biology of these sharks is poorly understood. In particular, it is unknown whether these species display genetically distinct populations throughout their ranges. Such information is necessary for effective management decisions in fisheries. We examined whether P. cirratus and P. nudipinnis display genetically distinct populations in the waters of southern Australia. Analysis of two mitochondrial genes (Cytochrome-b and ND5) indicated that the two species are structured differently, with P. cirratus consisting of two populations and P. nudipinnis consisting of one population. Tests for population expansion also highlighted differences between the species. Signatures of population expansion were detected in P. nudipinnis whilst P. cirratus showed an overall signature of stable population size, with evidence of expansion in one mitochondrial lineage. The observed population structure and expansion signatures are likely due to oceanographic changes in southern Australia during the Pleistocene. These results provide important information for management of sawsharks in commercial fisheries and demonstrate that population structure in closely related species within the same region can differ, and therefore requires investigation at the species level.

5989: Angel sharks (Squatinidae) are amongst the most threatened families of chondrichthyan species, with 13 of the 23 described species in a threat category. Reliance often falls on reports of incidental catch, citizen science, social media, and interviews with fishers to increase knowledge of distribution. Over recent years, in the wake of the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Angel Shark Conservation Strategy and inception of the Angel Shark Conservation Network, many more records have been unearthed from the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean. The Mediterranean Angel Sharks: Regional Action Plan sets out a roadmap for the three Critically Endangered species encountered in this region - Sawback Angelshark (Squatina aculeata), Smoothback Angelshark (S. oculata), and Angelshark (S. squatina). SubRegional Action Plans have since been developed for the Aegean Sea, Northern Levant Sea, Cyprus, Southern Ionian Sea and Tunisia, with a view to facilitating further coordinated action by engaging regional stakeholders (e.g. governments, industry) to better protect angel sharks. Varying levels of management and compliance in each region means key policy actions are adapted according to requirement. In working with regional partners, focus is on advancing policy developments, implementing existing regulations, and improving fisher awareness/engagement to reduce bycatch mortality. Collaborative action is essential to build capacity for angel shark conservation. Through the development of SubRegional Action Plans, along with the global angel shark ID guide, it’s hoped that a spotlight will be shone on this threatened family and highlight the importance of catch monitoring and management measures to prevent other species from following declining trends.

5990: Worldwide, angel sharks (family Squatinidae) are the third most threatened family of chondrichthyans. In the Southeast Pacific, two species are recorded: Squatina californica and Squatina armata. In Peru, between 1996 and 2001, the sixth most fished shark species was the S. californica. The catch of S. californica in Peru has declined by more than 90% between 2001 and 2020. A recent study conducted in Peru, confirmed the presence of S. californica and S. armata, and reported a potential third undescribed cryptic species (Squatina sp.). This study aimed to characterize the biology and fisheries of Squatina spp. in northern Peru. Five landing sites were evaluated between 2017 and 2019 (552 days). A total of 1,565 angelsharks were recorded (average total length 84.8 cm [SD=13.0, range: 27.7-101 cm], 56% female). Ninety-seven percent of the landings were from Puerto Pizarro (PP), the most northern site. Ninety-nine percent of the individuals landed in PP (n = 337) came from fishing areas in Ecuador. Tissue samples of 110 individuals were barcoded using the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I (COI) gene. Sixteen samples were identified as S. californica and 94 as S. sp. Most of the S. sp. samples were from Puerto Pizarro (n = 78). The results are concerning since direct capture of sharks has been prohibited in Ecuador since 2007. Moreover, the study highlights the need for accurate landing reports in Peru given the steep decline of the total catch of angelsharks.

5991: The white-spotted wedgefish (Rhynchobatus djiddensis) is a Critically Endangered shark-like ray in the family Rhinidae. Throughout its Western Indian Ocean distribution, it is targeted for its valuable meat and fins and is reported to have undergone major population declines. This study used two independent long-term (37 and 40 years) time-series catch data from competitive shore angling and shark nets to investigate the size composition and catch per unit effort (CPUE) and conduct a risk assessment for the population on the east coast of South Africa. From 1977 to 2017 the competitive shore fishery captured 7,703 individual R. djiddensis, whilst shark nets in the same region captured 2,856 individuals from1981 to 2017. Although the mean annual sizes of net-caught individuals were above the size of reported sexual maturity, there was little evidence to suggest that any individuals captured were reproductively active. Standardized CPUE from the competitive shore fishery declined substantially between 1977 and 2017 and shark net catches exhibited a significant (p< 0.05) fourfold decline in annual nominal CPUE from1981 to 2017. Ultimately, a risk assessment showed a 65.1% decline in abundance over a period of three generation lengths, which indicates that the sampled population of R. djiddensis in South Africa should be classified as Endangered. It is critical that the drivers of this population decline are identified and addressed to improve the conservation outcomes for this extremely vulnerable species.

5992: Understanding of species distribution and space-use is an essential prerequisite for effective marine conservation and management, and with a third of all chondrichthyan species now threatened with extinction, a chronic lack of data on basic ecology compounds extinction risk for many species. Squatina squatina (hereafter Angelshark), a bottom-dwelling coastal shark, is currently listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Despite recent conservation attention, there remains a significant lack of ecological data related to this species, and understanding of Angelshark behaviour, distribution and movement remains extremely limited. In the present study, acoustic telemetry was used to collect detailed data on movement, residency and space-use in adult Angelsharks within the La Graciosa Marine Reserve in the Canary Islands, with the aim of addressing key knowledge gaps and informing conservation policy. Between July 2018 and April 2022, 104 adult Angelsharks (72 females, 32 males) were tagged with acoustic transmitters and detected across 12 receivers. Significant sexual variation was found in space-use and seasonal presence in the study area, with results suggesting some localised sex-segregation outside of Winter months, when presence of both males and females peaked. While detections were concentrated in the shallow waters between La Graciosa and Lanzarote (up to 24m depth), notable use of an offshore location (86m depth) indicated utilisation of deep-water habitat, not previously observed in this species. The present findings have implications for Angelshark conservation, particularly in relation to sex-specific space-use and use of deep waters across the study area and more widely.

5993: The Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) is part of one of the most threatened families of elasmobranch (sharks, skates & rays) in the world. Despite a predicted 58% decline in their geographic extent over the last 50 years, a population remains off the coast of Wales, in the northernmost part of their range. Angel Shark Project: Wales (ASP:W) was launched in 2018 with the aim to safeguard Angelsharks in Wales with fishers and coastal communities, using heritage, education and research. Over the last five years, we have gathered 2,231 Angelshark records dating back to 1812 using a multidisciplinary approach via fisher engagement, archival research, digital platforms and a community roadshow across Wales. A combination of quantitative analysis, qualitative analysis and species distribution modelling have been used to interrogate the data and investigate Angelshark distribution and ecology in Wales. We will present key insights from these analyses, specifically the spatial and environmental trends in Angelshark distribution and what biological parameters may be driving these. We will also highlight the importance of integrating community voices and local ecological knowledge within the study of rare species, and how the results contribute towards delivering the Wales Angelshark Action Plan. 5994: Pelagic species presence at Manta Bowl in the TBPPS was investigated using remote underwater video surveys. Globally renowned as a reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi) cleaning station, this coastal seamount also hosts other endangered and protected species of megafauna including whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris), scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini), and pelagic thresher sharks (Alopias pelagicus). This study discusses the presence of pelagic thresher sharks at Manta Bowl. Pelagic thresher sharks are classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and are vulnerable to overexploitation. This study took place between August 2018 and August 2019, with 335 out of 384 days (87.2%) monitored. There was pelagic thresher shark presence on 120 of these days (35.8% of total days monitored) with a total of 211 thresher shark encounters determined over the study period. The study found that 43.6% of thresher shark encounters took place in the late morning, and seasonal peak was observed during the cool dry months of the Amihan season (52.1% of encounters were recorded between December and February). Despite the listing of pelagic thresher sharks in the CITES appendix II in 2016 and its subsequent implementation in 2017, both targeted and non-targeted catch of the species continues unmonitored and unmanaged. Considering the declaration of the protected status of the Ticao Burias Pass Protected Seascape in 2018, this seamount represents a key habitat for the conservation of this species. As such, fishery management interventions are urgently needed.

5995: Understanding residency patterns and space use of a species is key to implementation of sustainable and productive conservation management practices. Characterization of movement patterns of species within an ecosystem can provide insight into why animals use particular habitats, such as for feeding or reproduction, or how movements are regulated by various biotic or abiotic factors. Furthermore, by describing the fine scale movements of a species within an ecosystem, patterns of habitat use, movement corridors, and focal areas can be identified, at both the population or individual levels. Due to the logistical challenges of working in the Arctic, these types of studies have historically been limited compared to temperate or tropical climates. The Arctic Skate (Amblyraja hyperborea) is a high latitude, deep water species that is commonly caught as bycatch in both Canadian commercial and indigenous community fisheries. The life history characteristics of skates makes them vulnerable to overexploitation, and careful management is required. In this study, we used acoustic telemetry consisting of 81 receivers to study patterns of movement and residency of Arctic skates in Scott Inlet, Canada, the location of a developing community fishery for Greenland halibut. Our goal is to characterize residency patterns and space utilization of 52 skates across 6 years throughout the community fishing ground. The intent is to elucidate both how the skates distribute themselves within the region as well as identify how sex, size, and reproduction may impact these dynamics. Through understanding these movement metrics, bycatch of Arctic skate can be reduced and appropriate management formulated.
5996: Whale shark (Rhincodon typus) are listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The species is found globally in tropical and warm-temperate regions with high productivity. In the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) it can be found in coastal and offshore waters from the Gulf of California (Mexico) to the coast of Perú, including offshore islands, where its presence has been associated with primary productivity systems and oceanic fronts present in the region. This study aims to describe the effect of sea surface temperature, current velocity, chlorophyll-a and bathymetry on the habitat suitability of whale sharks at important aggregation sites in the ETP. A total of 93 individuals were tagged using satellite transmitters during expeditions carried out between 2011 and 2012 along ETP. A total of 2399 occurrence data were obtained, which were then used to create species niche models for the ETP using Maxent model. Sea surface temperature explained 42% of the suitable habitat, followed by chlorophyll-a and current velocity with 33.5% and 20.2% respectively. Finally, bathymetry accounted for 3.9% of the model. The habitat suitability index was high in areas close to the equatorial strip and change seasonally. The models indicate that suitable habitat is related to areas where non-directed fisheries can affect the shark, as well as other threats such as entanglements and ship strikes. This information contributes to the knowledge that should be considered in management measures for the conservation of the species.
5997: The Revillagigedo Archipelago is a region of great ecological importance, and it is considered a hub shark conservation. The presence of nine species of sharks in the area attracted diving activity within the park since 1980´s. The present study aims to determine the abundance of sharks using two methodologies: visual censuses (UVC) and baited underwater video stations (BRUVS), as well as to evaluate the effect of recreational diving on sharks. Relative abundances of various shark species per dive site and per sampling year (2015-2019) were calculated for UVCs and constrained by MaxN for BRUVS (2014). Contingency tables were made to determine significant differences in the abundance of the five most abundant shark species associated to site and year. Triaenodon obesus was the most abundant shark with 90% occurrence in 2018, followed by Sphyrna lewini 80% in 2015. We found significant differences (p<0.05) in the abundances related to the site and year of sampling. On the other hand, six species were recorded in the BRUVS, but only two were the most abundant: Carcharhinus albimarginatus and Carcharhinus falciformis. Roca Partida was the most sampled place with a total of 270 dives, followed by El Boiler with 139 dives. We found a higher probability of observing larger groups of sharks with smaller groups of divers, however, this was not significant. Therefore, the Revillagigedo archipelago serves as a refuge for different species of sharks, with Roca Partida being the site with the greatest abundance.
5998: Reef sharks have experienced widespread declines across much of the world’s coral reefs as a result of decades of overexploitation. Large knowledge gaps regarding the abundance of reef sharks worldwide have limited effective restoration and management of coastal shark populations. Although recent research has assessed the global status of reef sharks, it presents a snapshot in time with little indication of temporal variability in abundance. Identifying how seasonal changes in the environment influence abundance is important to ensure sampling is conducted at appropriate temporal scales to accurately quantify abundance, assess the role of reef sharks within communities and ecosystems, and ultimately implement suitable monitoring and management strategies. To explore seasonality in coastal reef shark populations worldwide, we used data from baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) in 371 sampling locations as part of a dedicated global survey across 58 countries, states, and territories. We developed a set of Bayesian hierarchical models that incorporate a continuous seasonal function to develop a predictive model of reef shark seasonality in abundance globally. Determining how seasonality influences reef shark abundance worldwide provides context to global catch records and abundance measures, allowing us to refine and standardize abundance estimates, and aiding in determining the most appropriate time of year for sampling.

5999: Despite the silky shark, Carcharhinus falciformis, being ubiquitous in tropical and sub-tropical pelagic waters and the second most common species found in the fin trade, little is known about its long-term horizontal movements. We tagged 40 silky sharks (7 males and 33 females) within the Galapagos Marine Reserve (GMR) with SPOT satellite tags during February and July 2021. Sharks were tracked for up to 374 days, with 25 sharks tracked for over 200 days and 18 sharks for over 300 days. All but one shark left the GMR, however, sharks were observed within the reserve during all months of the study and individuals were often in the reserve for months at a time. The number of sharks present within the reserve per month tended to decrease over the course of the year, but increased during February and March 2022, suggesting the Galapagos Islands may serve as a seasonal aggregation site. Female sharks leaving the reserve often displayed directional western movement traveling up to ~4000 km from the reserve. Despite large longitudinal movements, these movements were markedly latitudinally constrained, with most shark locations falling between the equator and 5˚ N latitude. Male sharks did not make long directional movements. Overall, for a wide-ranging species, silky sharks spent a great deal of time within the protected waters of the GMR, but their seasonal movements still put them at risk from commercial fisheries operating in the region, evidenced by the capture of three of the tagged sharks to date.
